kernelIdea: Axiom 5: 0 ∈ ℕ. Axiom 6: if x ∈ ℕ then S(x) ∈ ℕ. S is the next function; S(x) may not yet be written x + 1, because addition is not defined.

kernels.l1: Start at zero. Press the next button. That is all counting is.
kernels.l2: Counting starts at zero, and there is a machine that gives you the next one. The names one, two, three are just labels we chose for what the machine gives back.
kernels.l3: Two axioms build the counting numbers: zero is one of them, and every one of them has a next one. We define 1 to be the next after 0, and 2 to be the next after 1 — but we may not write S(x) as x + 1, because addition does not exist yet.
kernels.l4: Two axioms start the counting numbers: zero is one of them, and every one of them has a next one. The next-number machine is a function, and writing "next" as "add one" is forbidden at this stage — addition has not been defined yet.
kernels.l5: Zero and successor are the only primitives; the numerals are definitions, and no arithmetic may be assumed before it is constructed.
kernels.l6: The successor rule is a function in the sense of Chapter 3, and the discipline of this chapter is to assume nothing about it beyond the axioms.
kernels.l7: Two axioms introduce the only primitives: zero is a counting number, and every counting number has a next. The numerals are definitions, and *next* cannot be written as *add one* until addition has been constructed.
kernels.l8: Zero and successor generate the initial algebra for the functor X ↦ 1 + X; whether ℕ starts at 0 or 1 is a convention with no mathematical content.

kernel: Axiom 5: 0 ∈ ℕ. Axiom 6: if x ∈ ℕ then S(x) ∈ ℕ. S is the "next" function. We cannot yet call S(x) "x + 1" because + is not defined.
objectives: Explain why S(x) cannot yet be written x + 1
